input.rationale: The control case ran (CheckRun 7224dba1ed234879b0cb1c65e5161bf7, exit 0) and did what a control should: with the target still holding its vote, the same public call moved leadership to the named server (target_ever_leader=true, leaders_seen containing only the target, target_state_at_end=Leader, the original leader in Follower at the end) with the term advancing by exactly one, 2 to 3. Set against the vote-less case (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227: target_suffrage=Nonvoter, target_ever_leader=false, term 2 to 4), the pair removes the competing explanation that the transfer mechanism simply does not work in this harness, and it makes the cost difference concrete: the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the transfer campaign plus the re-election that recovered leadership) while moving authority nowhere, and the caller received the same empty error in both cases. That last point is a correction to my own earlier phrasing: an empty transfer error is not by itself evidence of a failed transfer, since the successful control also reports none; the discriminating operands are who led and how the term moved. I record the control observation as a fact, state the current account for the question in one interpretation that links both receipts and says plainly what remains open, and queue one repeat of the vote-less experiment to see whether the non-transfer and its term cost reproduce under a fresh schedule rather than resting on a single run.

knowledge.statement: On one real four-node cluster where the named transfer target held its vote (target_suffrage=Voter), LeadershipTransferToServer moved leadership to that named server: the target was the only server observed in Leader state, it was in Leader state at the end, the original leader ended in Follower state without leading again, and the maximum term advanced by one, from 2 to 3. The caller's future reported no error, the same empty value reported for the vote-less target in the paired case.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with no configuration change before the transfer; target chosen from nodes in Follower state; observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms; separate execution from the vote-less case, same harness shape and cluster shape.

interpretations.rationale: The control predicate was that the same call with a voter as the named target does move leadership to that server, and it holds: the target was the only leader observed, ended in Leader state, the original leader ended in Follower and never led again, and the term moved 2 to 3, a single step. That matters twice over for the question about vote-less targets. First, it removes the alternative that the explicit transfer path is simply inoperative in this harness, because the identical call delivered leadership when the target had a vote; combined with the source facts that a non-voter casts no self-vote (a vote is cast only for servers whose suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), that voters reject its RequestVote after adopting its higher term (raft.go:1664-1684), and that a non-voter never starts an election by itself (raft.go:242-250), the failure to transfer is attributable to the target's lacking a vote rather than to the harness or to the call. Second, it makes the cost of the vote-less attempt visible relative to the intended path: the successful transfer advanced the term by one and placed the named server in charge, while the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the campaign at term 3 and the re-election at term 4 seen in that run's log) and left the same server as a follower, so the request consumed an extra election and returned no benefit. It also corrects my earlier emphasis: transfer_err was empty in both cases, so the empty error is not what marks the failure - in the control it accompanies success. The discriminating evidence is the pair of outcomes (target_ever_leader true with one term step, versus false with two term steps) plus the two source arguments, and the caller-visible gap remains that both callers receive the same success signal while only one of them had authority moved to the named node. The current account is therefore unchanged in substance and better bounded: the defect is that the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership and reports success, and I keep the residual uncertainty about timing variation rather than smoothing it away, which is what the queued repeat of the vote-less case examines.
counterevidence: The two cases are separate executions on separate clusters, not a randomized paired trial, so run-to-run timing variation is not excluded by the pair alone; what the pair excludes is the specific alternative that the transfer mechanism does not work in this harness, and the queued repeat tests whether the vote-less non-transfer and its two-step term cost recur.
An empty transfer error occurs in both cases, so it cannot be used as the distinguishing signal; the earlier account leaned on that value and is narrowed here to the outcome and term-cost operands.

In the control the original leader ended as a follower without leading again, while in the vote-less case leadership stayed with the original server; a caller watching only the final leader could therefore see the vote-less request as harmless, and the harm is the wasted election cycle rather than a lasting loss.
limitations: Each case is a single execution with a single target chosen among followers; neither case repeats a target of the other suffrage type more than once, so the comparison rests on two runs plus the source paths.

The 3 s window bounds what is observed; the claim that a vote-less member can never win is source-based, and the term-movement comparison is an endpoint-to-endpoint difference, not a trace of every intermediate term value.

The vote-less case's target had been demoted by the caller in the same run, so the configuration change and the transfer are not separated in time in that execution; the control has no such change, which is a second difference between the two runs besides suffrage.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the vote-less case are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters of the same shape (MakeCluster(4) with default config, one elected leader, a follower chosen from Follower state as target, 3 s sampling every 20 ms). They differ in exactly one input: in the vote-less case the target is first demoted by a committed DemoteVoter, in the control it keeps its vote. They are independent executions rather than one split history, so the pair supports a same-cause comparison (transition works with a vote, does not deliver without one) and does not by itself exclude run-to-run timing variation.

knowledge.statement: Raft.GetConfiguration() returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations field carries only latest (the atomic latestConfiguration copy), and ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns configurations.latestIndex, so the value a caller receives from Index() is 0 on every call regardless of the cluster's committed or latest configuration index. The authoritative index r.configurations.latestIndex lives only on the main thread and reaches callers solely through the configurationsCh request path (raft.go:882-890, snapshot.go:155).
knowledge.conditions: Any Raft instance, running or started with skipStartup (including the package-level GetConfiguration helper, api.go:445-458 which the doc claims has identical behavior); GetConfiguration is documented as returning the latest configuration, which may be uncommitted.

knowledge.statement: Raft.Stats() sets latest_configuration_index from the future returned by GetConfiguration(), so the published value is the constant string "0" even on a bootstrapped cluster whose configuration entry sits at index >= 1, while the same future supplies a non-empty latest_configuration. A Stats() consumer therefore cannot distinguish clusters by configuration index, and the key is constant rather than observed.
knowledge.conditions: Any node that serves Stats() while its GetConfiguration branch runs; applies to leader and follower alike.

knowledge.statement: nextConfiguration applies the caller's precondition only when change.prevIndex > 0; AddVoter/AddNonvoter/RemoveServer/DemoteVoter pass the caller-supplied prevIndex through unchanged, so passing 0 (the value the public API returns for the configuration index) silently converts a conditional configuration change into an unconditional one.
knowledge.conditions: The leader-loop configuration change path of this revision; requires the caller to have obtained prevIndex from the public API.

knowledge.statement: On one running bootstrapped three-node cluster (term 2, commit_index 3, applied_index 3), the elected leader's main thread held configuration index 1 (latest and committed, 3 voter servers), while the same instance's public GetConfiguration().Index() was 0 with Configuration() returning the same 3 voter servers, and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] was "0" next to a non-empty latest_configuration. The value handed to API callers is therefore not the node's configuration index.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028, sampled while exactly one node was in Leader state, MakeCluster(3) bootstrap in one process with one committed client command.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration, so Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest index
Stats() publishes latest_configuration_index from the same future, i.e. the constant "0"

knowledge.statement: Apply/ApplyLog and Barrier use the caller's timeout only in the select that enqueues the logFuture into applyCh; the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh (only internal restore and snapshot futures set one, raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152), so once the send succeeds the caller's Error() waits on the internal error channel alone and neither the timeout nor Shutdown() bounds completion.
knowledge.conditions: Any caller that keeps the future returned by Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier; the window requires acceptance to succeed, which BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174) permits without a consumer, and its documentation already states that it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply.

knowledge.statement: Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown but does not drain or respond to futures already queued in applyCh; the main loop leaves its select on shutdownCh and run() returns, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight, so a duty that reached the buffer but was never dispatched has no remaining producer to complete it.
knowledge.conditions: Applies whenever a logFuture was accepted into applyCh while the main loop was occupied elsewhere and the node is then shut down; the repository's own test file already notes stuck Barrier/VerifyLeader/GetConfiguration futures after shutdown at raft_test.go:40-42.

knowledge.statement: On one real bootstrapped three-node cluster with BatchApplyCh enabled, a Barrier future handed to the caller by the public API while the leader was occupied inside its own Restore handler was never responded after Shutdown(): the node moved from state Leader at acceptance to state Shutdown, the duty remained queued in applyCh (queued_in_apply_ch=1, capacity 64) and the future's Error() had not returned after the bounded 3000 ms observation. The control Barrier on the undisturbed leader returned no error, and the occupied handler resumed afterwards (restore returned 'failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF').
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(3) with conf.BatchApplyCh=true; the main loop occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls on its first Read at the moment the Barrier is accepted; Shutdown() called after acceptance and before any consumer drains applyCh.

knowledge.assertion: Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier use the timeout only for the enqueue and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so acceptance is not followed by any timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion

Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already on leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in the buffer has no remaining producer

knowledge.statement: On one real four-node cluster whose named transfer target held no vote (target_suffrage=Nonvoter), LeadershipTransferToServer returned a future reporting no error, the named target never reached Leader in the 3 s observation window and ended in state Follower, the maximum cluster term advanced from 2 to 4, and the only server observed leading was the original leader, which was in Leader state at the end. The requested transfer of authority to the named server therefore did not take effect and was not reported as a failure.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with the target demoted by a committed DemoteVoter in the same run; target chosen from nodes in Follower state and still replicated to by the leader; Observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms.

interpretations.rationale: Source reading fixes the mechanism without needing a measurement: GetConfiguration() responds a configurationsFuture built from configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} (api.go:900) and getLatestConfiguration only loads the Configuration, not its index (raft.go:2232-2240); Index() is then latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270), i.e. 0. The real index is available in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so this is not a case where the information does not exist, but one where the public producer drops it. The consumer duty is concrete and documented: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry', future.go:27-33), and the documented use of that index is the configuration compare-and-swap: AddVoter and friends describe prevIndex as 'the index of the only configuration upon which this change may be applied; if another configuration entry has been added in the meantime, this request will fail' (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as 'no precondition' (configuration.go:229), so the guard is silently disabled - the request loses the very protection the API promises, and the loss is invisible because the call still succeeds. The same zero is republished as latest_configuration_index in Stats() (api.go:1188), where a constant '0' also misrepresents the node's configuration state to operators. The pending harness (assurance_generated_test.go) is the discriminating observation: it samples the public values next to the main-thread latestIndex on one running bootstrapped leader, which will either confirm the constant zero or defeat the account. Implications are scoped to callers that rely on the index (CAS preconditions, correlating a configuration with a log position); the configuration contents themselves are live and correct, so this is not a consensus-safety defect.
limitations: No execution yet in this turn: the account rests on source reasoning and on the documented API meaning; the harness has been written but has not run, so the observed value is still unknown.
Severity is bounded: callers that ignore Index() are unaffected, and the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was: if the public values track the real index the hypothesis is wrong, if the public values stay 0 while the main-thread index is >= 1 it holds. The completed execution reports exactly the second case on one node and one sample: main_latest_index=1 and main_committed_index=1 (3 voter servers) read from the main thread, public_index=0 with public_servers=3 read from GetConfiguration(), and stats_latest_configuration_index="0" beside the same three-voter latest_configuration, with commit_index=3 and applied_index=3 showing the node was well past the configuration entry. Both values came from the same runtime object inside one execution, so this is a within-node comparison rather than a cross-scenario join. The account of why is source-fixed and independent of the sample: GetConfiguration() constructs configurationsFuture{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} and responds it immediately (api.go:900), getLatestConfiguration loads only the Configuration from the atomic copy (raft.go:2232-2240), and Index() is the never-assigned latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270); no code path assigns it for this future, so the constant is a property of the constructor rather than an artefact of one sample. The real index does exist in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so the public producer drops a value the target itself publishes elsewhere. The consumer duty is what makes this consequential rather than cosmetic: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry'), and the documented use of that index is the configuration precondition - AddVoter and its siblings describe prevIndex as the index of the only configuration upon which the change may be applied, failing if another configuration entry intervened (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as no precondition (configuration.go:229), so the request keeps the same return value while silently losing the protection it was composed around; the same 0 is republished as latest_configuration_index (api.go:1188), where a constant also misdescribes the node's configuration state to an operator. Scope is bounded and stated: the configuration contents are live and correct and no consensus decision is taken on this value, so this is a basis/contract defect for index-dependent callers, not a safety violation.

answers.031156ce4e3d4bf5a8845619024ff0c4-gap-0: Observed on the elected leader of a bootstrapped three-node cluster (CheckRun dd34591ecee5442ca8f7b8c478709f1b, parsed event 0): GetConfiguration().Index() carried 0 while the main thread's latest and committed configuration index for the same node was 1 with 3 voter servers, and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] carried the same "0" beside a non-empty latest_configuration; the public value does not track the real index.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration (latestIndex left zero), so ConfigurationFuture.Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest configuration index
nextConfiguration enforces prevIndex only when it is > 0, so the 0 returned by the public API disables the documented configuration compare-and-swap

counterevidence: The captured tree is byte-identical to the released upstream copy of the same revision, and no assertion or test in the snapshot requires ConfigurationFuture.Index() to be non-zero, so the judgment that the zero is a defect rather than an intended 'there is no index to report here' reading rests on the documented meaning of Index() and of prevIndex rather than on a violated in-tree expectation.

The witness is one node in one execution; the claim that the value is constant rests on the constructor and on the absence of any writer to that field for this future (api.go:895-903, future.go:255-270), not on repeated sampling.
limitations: Only the index value is shown to be wrong; the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration, and callers that ignore Index() are unaffected.
The impact chain to the disabled precondition is source-based: the execution exercised the read path, not a configuration change issued with the returned 0 as prevIndex.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved in the direction that supports the defect account, and the decisive operands come from one instance in one execution rather than from a join across scenarios: control_barrier_err is empty (the same Barrier call completed on the undisturbed leader, so acceptance and completion work when a producer exists), freeze_handshake is inside_restore_read (the main loop was inside its own restore handler and could not select on applyCh again), state_at_accept is Leader and duty_accepted is true (the public API handed the caller a future), state_after_shutdown is Shutdown, and the observation reports result=no_completion over a 3000 ms interval with queued_in_apply_ch=1 and apply_ch_capacity=64 - the accepted duty was still sitting in the buffer, with no consumer, after authority was lost. restore_after_release='failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF' shows that the occupied handler was the node's main loop and that it did resume once the reader was released, which also rules out the harness having wedged the node in some other way. The interval is stated as what it is: 3000 ms of non-progress is not by itself the evidence for indefinite blocking; the indefinite part is source-fixed, and it is why the future can never be woken - deferError.Error() waits on the internal error channel alone once respond has not been called (future.go:113-118), and this logFuture is created without a ShutdownCh, unlike the internal restore and snapshot futures that do get one (raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152); Shutdown() only closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown (api.go:1012-1025) while both the main loop and runFSM leave on that channel; and runLeader's defer responds only the futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight (raft.go:502-560), which a duty that never left applyCh is not. The duty was therefore accepted, its basis (a live leader to dispatch it) disappeared, and the accepted obligation was neither cancelled with a reason nor transferred: it was dropped silently, which is exactly the failure the repository's own test file flags for this family at raft_test.go:40-42. The condition that makes it reachable is the documented one: BatchApplyCh decouples acceptance from consumption (config.go:169-174), and the same comment concedes it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply, so a caller that trusts a positive timeout to bound its wait is not protected.

answers.f2c2b4e0415449d4941c8e53ffbc722e-gap-1: No producer responded the accepted Barrier future after Shutdown(), and the duty was still queued at that point: with the leader occupied inside its own Restore handler, the Barrier future was accepted in state Leader and, after Shutdown() moved the node to state Shutdown, the future had not been responded within the 3000 ms observation while len(applyCh)=1 of capacity 64 (CheckRun c5d127c955b549a8888fe6bab568dbce, parsed event 0).

knowledge.assertion: the timeout guards only the enqueue into applyCh and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so no timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion follows acceptance
Shutdown() leaves applyCh undrained and runLeader's defer responds only leaderState.inflight futures, so the queued duty has no remaining producer

counterevidence: The reachable window needs the main loop to be occupied at the moment of acceptance and shutdown; the harness makes that deterministic with a caller-supplied reader that stalls, so the execution shows the mechanism, not a frequency of occurrence under spontaneous timing.

The window also needs BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174); with the default unbuffered applyCh the enqueue itself is the handoff, so the same duty would instead be rejected at enqueue via the caller's timeout or shutdownCh escape in Apply.

The node was in the middle of an orderly shutdown, so one can argue a shutting-down node owes nothing in flight; the defect account rests on the narrower observation that the API had already accepted the duty and returned a future whose Error() has no shutdown notice and no timeout, leaving the caller unable to distinguish dropped from pending.
limitations: Single node and single execution; the claim that no completion path remains rests on the source argument above (no writer to the error channel after shutdown; every completer exits on shutdownCh), not on repeated sampling or on an unbounded wait.

Only the Barrier path was executed. VerifyLeader constructs its verifyFuture without a ShutdownCh too and sends it on a 64-buffered channel (api.go:883-893, api.go:568), so it shares the shape, but that is a source-level observation and was not exercised.
The scenario models a slow caller-supplied stream keeping the handler busy; it does not claim that shutdown always finds a duty in the buffer.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved against the harmless reading: the named target never reached Leader, so the transfer did not accomplish what the API call names. The decisive operands from that one execution are target_suffrage=Nonvoter (the target really held no vote, confirmed from the leader's latest configuration), transfer_err empty (the caller was told the transfer was not a failure), target_ever_leader=false with target_state_at_end=Follower, leaders_seen containing only the original leader, and term_before=2 to term_after=4. The impossibility is source-fixed and independent of the window: a server without a vote has no self-vote in electSelf (a vote is cast only when the iterated server's Suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), voters reject its RequestVote after the term adoption that precedes the rejection (raft.go:1664-1684), and a non-voter never starts an election on its own (raft.go:242-250) - so no vote-less member can ever be elected in this revision, and the explicit transfer path accepted one anyway because it only looks for a replication state (raft.go:765-783). The cost side is what the term movement shows: the transfer candidate ran a real election (TimeoutNow sets Candidate and the transfer flag, raft.go:2209-2214, and that flag suppresses pre-vote in the candidate loop, raft.go:294-300), voters adopted the higher term and stepped down before rejecting, and with the term at 4 the sitting leader at term 2 cannot still have been leader, so leadership was lost and had to be re-won. The asymmetry with the implicit path, which deliberately skips non-voters when picking a server (raft.go:2163-2182), shows the explicit input is accepted where the implicit path would have refused it. The report to the caller is the part that turns this from an operator mistake into a defect of the library: the transfer case answers nil when leadership is lost during a transfer because that is the expected outcome (raft.go:734-739), so a caller that named a vote-less server receives the same success signal as a caller whose transfer worked, and cannot tell that authority never reached the named node.

answers.721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-gap-2: No: the named vote-less target never acquired leadership (target_ever_leader=false over the 3 s window, ending in state Follower) while the caller's future reported no error (transfer_err empty), and the cluster's maximum term advanced from 2 to 4 with the original leader in Leader state at the end (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227, parsed event 0). Source shows the negative is structural: a non-voter gets no self-vote and voters reject its request.

counterevidence: This execution contains no same-window control, so the term advance is attributed to the transfer campaign on the source argument that a Leader never campaigns itself and that a voter adopts a higher term before rejecting it; the control just queued (same path, voter target) separates 'the mechanism does not work here' from 'the mechanism works and a vote-less target cannot take the leadership', but it does not by itself exclude spontaneous election noise in a 3 s window.

The end state is the same as the start (the original leader leads again), so a caller that inspects only who leads afterwards sees no damage; the observed harm is the term movement and the inferred loss of leadership in between, not a lasting loss.

The target's vote was removed by the caller's own previous API call in the same run, so this is not a case where the library silently mis-states an operator-managed configuration; the operator asked for the demotion, then asked for a transfer to the demoted node.
limitations: Single execution and a single target; the claim that a vote-less member can never win rests on the election code paths above, not on repeated runs.

The caller's success value is explained by the lost-leadership branch (raft.go:734-739); the same CheckRun's DEBUG log names that branch ('lost leadership during transfer (expected)'), which corroborates the reading but is the library's own message text rather than an independent probe of the returned value.

The intermediate sequence is observed in the run's own log rather than merely inferred: at 16:26:25.836 the target enters candidate state at term=3 with no pre-vote success line and asks all three voters for a vote while never logging a self-vote, each voter logs term adoption ('lost leadership because received a requestVote with a newer term') immediately followed by 'rejecting vote request since node is not a voter: from=927e473c...', and at 16:26:25.894 the original leader campaigns at term=4 (pre-vote tally 2 of votesNeeded 2) and re-enters leader state; these are the library's own log messages, while the sampled CA_EVENT operands remain the states, term endpoints and window.

Because the term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while both genuine elections in the same run recorded a successful pre-vote first, the log also distinguishes the transfer path from an ordinary election; what it does not provide is a run of the same window without the transfer call, which is why the control case is queued rather than assumed.

result.summary: The control case ran (CheckRun 7224dba1ed234879b0cb1c65e5161bf7, exit 0) and behaved as a control should: with the target still holding its vote, the same public call moved leadership to the named server - target_ever_leader=true, the target the only leader seen and in Leader state at the end, the original leader in Follower and never leading again - with the term advancing by exactly one, from 2 to 3. Set against the vote-less case (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227: target_suffrage=Nonvoter, target_ever_leader=false, term 2 to 4), the pair removes the alternative that the explicit transfer path is simply inoperative in this harness and makes the cost contrast concrete: the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the transfer campaign plus the re-election that recovered leadership) while moving authority nowhere. It also corrects my own earlier emphasis, which I have narrowed in the record: an empty transfer error cannot be the distinguishing signal, because the successful control reports the same empty value; what discriminates is who led and how the term moved. I recorded the control observation as a fact, wrote one interpretation that links both receipts with joint_history explaining they are same-shape separate executions differing in exactly one input (the target's suffrage, and in the vote-less run also the caller's prior demotion), and kept three counterweights and three limits - most importantly that a pair of separate runs does not exclude timing variation, and that neither case was repeated for its target type. To close that last gap I queued a repeat of the vote-less experiment, whose purpose is to see whether the non-transfer and its two-step term cost recur under a fresh schedule. Earlier witnessed findings on the configuration index and on duties lost at shutdown remain recorded and are unaffected by this turn.

knowledge.statement: On one real bootstrapped three-node cluster with BatchApplyCh enabled, a Barrier future handed to the caller by the public API while the leader was occupied inside its own Restore handler was never responded after Shutdown(): the node moved from state Leader at acceptance to state Shutdown, the duty remained queued in applyCh (queued_in_apply_ch=1, capacity 64) and the future's Error() had not returned after the bounded 3000 ms observation. The control Barrier on the undisturbed leader returned no error, and the occupied handler resumed afterwards (restore returned 'failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF').
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(3) with conf.BatchApplyCh=true; the main loop occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls on its first Read at the moment the Barrier is accepted; Shutdown() called after acceptance and before any consumer drains applyCh.

knowledge.assertion: Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier use the timeout only for the enqueue and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so acceptance is not followed by any timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion

Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already on leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in the buffer has no remaining producer

knowledge.statement: On one real four-node cluster whose named transfer target held no vote (target_suffrage=Nonvoter), LeadershipTransferToServer returned a future reporting no error, the named target never reached Leader in the 3 s observation window and ended in state Follower, the maximum cluster term advanced from 2 to 4, and the only server observed leading was the original leader, which was in Leader state at the end. The requested transfer of authority to the named server therefore did not take effect and was not reported as a failure.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with the target demoted by a committed DemoteVoter in the same run; target chosen from nodes in Follower state and still replicated to by the leader; Observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms.

knowledge.statement: On one real four-node cluster where the named transfer target held its vote (target_suffrage=Voter), LeadershipTransferToServer moved leadership to that named server: the target was the only server observed in Leader state, it was in Leader state at the end, the original leader ended in Follower state without leading again, and the maximum term advanced by one, from 2 to 3. The caller's future reported no error, the same empty value reported for the vote-less target in the paired case.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with no configuration change before the transfer; target chosen from nodes in Follower state; observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms; separate execution from the vote-less case, same harness shape and cluster shape.

interpretations.rationale: Source reading fixes the mechanism without needing a measurement: GetConfiguration() responds a configurationsFuture built from configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} (api.go:900) and getLatestConfiguration only loads the Configuration, not its index (raft.go:2232-2240); Index() is then latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270), i.e. 0. The real index is available in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so this is not a case where the information does not exist, but one where the public producer drops it. The consumer duty is concrete and documented: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry', future.go:27-33), and the documented use of that index is the configuration compare-and-swap: AddVoter and friends describe prevIndex as 'the index of the only configuration upon which this change may be applied; if another configuration entry has been added in the meantime, this request will fail' (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as 'no precondition' (configuration.go:229), so the guard is silently disabled - the request loses the very protection the API promises, and the loss is invisible because the call still succeeds. The same zero is republished as latest_configuration_index in Stats() (api.go:1188), where a constant '0' also misrepresents the node's configuration state to operators. The pending harness (assurance_generated_test.go) is the discriminating observation: it samples the public values next to the main-thread latestIndex on one running bootstrapped leader, which will either confirm the constant zero or defeat the account. Implications are scoped to callers that rely on the index (CAS preconditions, correlating a configuration with a log position); the configuration contents themselves are live and correct, so this is not a consensus-safety defect.
limitations: No execution yet in this turn: the account rests on source reasoning and on the documented API meaning; the harness has been written but has not run, so the observed value is still unknown.
Severity is bounded: callers that ignore Index() are unaffected, and the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was: if the public values track the real index the hypothesis is wrong, if the public values stay 0 while the main-thread index is >= 1 it holds. The completed execution reports exactly the second case on one node and one sample: main_latest_index=1 and main_committed_index=1 (3 voter servers) read from the main thread, public_index=0 with public_servers=3 read from GetConfiguration(), and stats_latest_configuration_index="0" beside the same three-voter latest_configuration, with commit_index=3 and applied_index=3 showing the node was well past the configuration entry. Both values came from the same runtime object inside one execution, so this is a within-node comparison rather than a cross-scenario join. The account of why is source-fixed and independent of the sample: GetConfiguration() constructs configurationsFuture{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} and responds it immediately (api.go:900), getLatestConfiguration loads only the Configuration from the atomic copy (raft.go:2232-2240), and Index() is the never-assigned latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270); no code path assigns it for this future, so the constant is a property of the constructor rather than an artefact of one sample. The real index does exist in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so the public producer drops a value the target itself publishes elsewhere. The consumer duty is what makes this consequential rather than cosmetic: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry'), and the documented use of that index is the configuration precondition - AddVoter and its siblings describe prevIndex as the index of the only configuration upon which the change may be applied, failing if another configuration entry intervened (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as no precondition (configuration.go:229), so the request keeps the same return value while silently losing the protection it was composed around; the same 0 is republished as latest_configuration_index (api.go:1188), where a constant also misdescribes the node's configuration state to an operator. Scope is bounded and stated: the configuration contents are live and correct and no consensus decision is taken on this value, so this is a basis/contract defect for index-dependent callers, not a safety violation.

answers.031156ce4e3d4bf5a8845619024ff0c4-gap-0: Observed on the elected leader of a bootstrapped three-node cluster (CheckRun dd34591ecee5442ca8f7b8c478709f1b, parsed event 0): GetConfiguration().Index() carried 0 while the main thread's latest and committed configuration index for the same node was 1 with 3 voter servers, and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] carried the same "0" beside a non-empty latest_configuration; the public value does not track the real index.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration (latestIndex left zero), so ConfigurationFuture.Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest configuration index
nextConfiguration enforces prevIndex only when it is > 0, so the 0 returned by the public API disables the documented configuration compare-and-swap

counterevidence: The captured tree is byte-identical to the released upstream copy of the same revision, and no assertion or test in the snapshot requires ConfigurationFuture.Index() to be non-zero, so the judgment that the zero is a defect rather than an intended 'there is no index to report here' reading rests on the documented meaning of Index() and of prevIndex rather than on a violated in-tree expectation.

The witness is one node in one execution; the claim that the value is constant rests on the constructor and on the absence of any writer to that field for this future (api.go:895-903, future.go:255-270), not on repeated sampling.
limitations: Only the index value is shown to be wrong; the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration, and callers that ignore Index() are unaffected.
The impact chain to the disabled precondition is source-based: the execution exercised the read path, not a configuration change issued with the returned 0 as prevIndex.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved in the direction that supports the defect account, and the decisive operands come from one instance in one execution rather than from a join across scenarios: control_barrier_err is empty (the same Barrier call completed on the undisturbed leader, so acceptance and completion work when a producer exists), freeze_handshake is inside_restore_read (the main loop was inside its own restore handler and could not select on applyCh again), state_at_accept is Leader and duty_accepted is true (the public API handed the caller a future), state_after_shutdown is Shutdown, and the observation reports result=no_completion over a 3000 ms interval with queued_in_apply_ch=1 and apply_ch_capacity=64 - the accepted duty was still sitting in the buffer, with no consumer, after authority was lost. restore_after_release='failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF' shows that the occupied handler was the node's main loop and that it did resume once the reader was released, which also rules out the harness having wedged the node in some other way. The interval is stated as what it is: 3000 ms of non-progress is not by itself the evidence for indefinite blocking; the indefinite part is source-fixed, and it is why the future can never be woken - deferError.Error() waits on the internal error channel alone once respond has not been called (future.go:113-118), and this logFuture is created without a ShutdownCh, unlike the internal restore and snapshot futures that do get one (raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152); Shutdown() only closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown (api.go:1012-1025) while both the main loop and runFSM leave on that channel; and runLeader's defer responds only the futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight (raft.go:502-560), which a duty that never left applyCh is not. The duty was therefore accepted, its basis (a live leader to dispatch it) disappeared, and the accepted obligation was neither cancelled with a reason nor transferred: it was dropped silently, which is exactly the failure the repository's own test file flags for this family at raft_test.go:40-42. The condition that makes it reachable is the documented one: BatchApplyCh decouples acceptance from consumption (config.go:169-174), and the same comment concedes it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply, so a caller that trusts a positive timeout to bound its wait is not protected.

answers.f2c2b4e0415449d4941c8e53ffbc722e-gap-1: No producer responded the accepted Barrier future after Shutdown(), and the duty was still queued at that point: with the leader occupied inside its own Restore handler, the Barrier future was accepted in state Leader and, after Shutdown() moved the node to state Shutdown, the future had not been responded within the 3000 ms observation while len(applyCh)=1 of capacity 64 (CheckRun c5d127c955b549a8888fe6bab568dbce, parsed event 0).

knowledge.assertion: the timeout guards only the enqueue into applyCh and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so no timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion follows acceptance
Shutdown() leaves applyCh undrained and runLeader's defer responds only leaderState.inflight futures, so the queued duty has no remaining producer

counterevidence: The reachable window needs the main loop to be occupied at the moment of acceptance and shutdown; the harness makes that deterministic with a caller-supplied reader that stalls, so the execution shows the mechanism, not a frequency of occurrence under spontaneous timing.

The window also needs BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174); with the default unbuffered applyCh the enqueue itself is the handoff, so the same duty would instead be rejected at enqueue via the caller's timeout or shutdownCh escape in Apply.

The node was in the middle of an orderly shutdown, so one can argue a shutting-down node owes nothing in flight; the defect account rests on the narrower observation that the API had already accepted the duty and returned a future whose Error() has no shutdown notice and no timeout, leaving the caller unable to distinguish dropped from pending.
limitations: Single node and single execution; the claim that no completion path remains rests on the source argument above (no writer to the error channel after shutdown; every completer exits on shutdownCh), not on repeated sampling or on an unbounded wait.

Only the Barrier path was executed. VerifyLeader constructs its verifyFuture without a ShutdownCh too and sends it on a 64-buffered channel (api.go:883-893, api.go:568), so it shares the shape, but that is a source-level observation and was not exercised.
The scenario models a slow caller-supplied stream keeping the handler busy; it does not claim that shutdown always finds a duty in the buffer.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved against the harmless reading: the named target never reached Leader, so the transfer did not accomplish what the API call names. The decisive operands from that one execution are target_suffrage=Nonvoter (the target really held no vote, confirmed from the leader's latest configuration), transfer_err empty (the caller was told the transfer was not a failure), target_ever_leader=false with target_state_at_end=Follower, leaders_seen containing only the original leader, and term_before=2 to term_after=4. The impossibility is source-fixed and independent of the window: a server without a vote has no self-vote in electSelf (a vote is cast only when the iterated server's Suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), voters reject its RequestVote after the term adoption that precedes the rejection (raft.go:1664-1684), and a non-voter never starts an election on its own (raft.go:242-250) - so no vote-less member can ever be elected in this revision, and the explicit transfer path accepted one anyway because it only looks for a replication state (raft.go:765-783). The cost side is what the term movement shows: the transfer candidate ran a real election (TimeoutNow sets Candidate and the transfer flag, raft.go:2209-2214, and that flag suppresses pre-vote in the candidate loop, raft.go:294-300), voters adopted the higher term and stepped down before rejecting, and with the term at 4 the sitting leader at term 2 cannot still have been leader, so leadership was lost and had to be re-won. The asymmetry with the implicit path, which deliberately skips non-voters when picking a server (raft.go:2163-2182), shows the explicit input is accepted where the implicit path would have refused it. The report to the caller is the part that turns this from an operator mistake into a defect of the library: the transfer case answers nil when leadership is lost during a transfer because that is the expected outcome (raft.go:734-739), so a caller that named a vote-less server receives the same success signal as a caller whose transfer worked, and cannot tell that authority never reached the named node.

answers.721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-gap-2: No: the named vote-less target never acquired leadership (target_ever_leader=false over the 3 s window, ending in state Follower) while the caller's future reported no error (transfer_err empty), and the cluster's maximum term advanced from 2 to 4 with the original leader in Leader state at the end (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227, parsed event 0). Source shows the negative is structural: a non-voter gets no self-vote and voters reject its request.

counterevidence: This execution contains no same-window control, so the term advance is attributed to the transfer campaign on the source argument that a Leader never campaigns itself and that a voter adopts a higher term before rejecting it; the control just queued (same path, voter target) separates 'the mechanism does not work here' from 'the mechanism works and a vote-less target cannot take the leadership', but it does not by itself exclude spontaneous election noise in a 3 s window.

The end state is the same as the start (the original leader leads again), so a caller that inspects only who leads afterwards sees no damage; the observed harm is the term movement and the inferred loss of leadership in between, not a lasting loss.

The target's vote was removed by the caller's own previous API call in the same run, so this is not a case where the library silently mis-states an operator-managed configuration; the operator asked for the demotion, then asked for a transfer to the demoted node.
limitations: Single execution and a single target; the claim that a vote-less member can never win rests on the election code paths above, not on repeated runs.

The caller's success value is explained by the lost-leadership branch (raft.go:734-739); the same CheckRun's DEBUG log names that branch ('lost leadership during transfer (expected)'), which corroborates the reading but is the library's own message text rather than an independent probe of the returned value.

The intermediate sequence is observed in the run's own log rather than merely inferred: at 16:26:25.836 the target enters candidate state at term=3 with no pre-vote success line and asks all three voters for a vote while never logging a self-vote, each voter logs term adoption ('lost leadership because received a requestVote with a newer term') immediately followed by 'rejecting vote request since node is not a voter: from=927e473c...', and at 16:26:25.894 the original leader campaigns at term=4 (pre-vote tally 2 of votesNeeded 2) and re-enters leader state; these are the library's own log messages, while the sampled CA_EVENT operands remain the states, term endpoints and window.

Because the term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while both genuine elections in the same run recorded a successful pre-vote first, the log also distinguishes the transfer path from an ordinary election; what it does not provide is a run of the same window without the transfer call, which is why the control case is queued rather than assumed.

interpretations.rationale: The control predicate was that the same call with a voter as the named target does move leadership to that server, and it holds: the target was the only leader observed, ended in Leader state, the original leader ended in Follower and never led again, and the term moved 2 to 3, a single step. That matters twice over for the question about vote-less targets. First, it removes the alternative that the explicit transfer path is simply inoperative in this harness, because the identical call delivered leadership when the target had a vote; combined with the source facts that a non-voter casts no self-vote (a vote is cast only for servers whose suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), that voters reject its RequestVote after adopting its higher term (raft.go:1664-1684), and that a non-voter never starts an election by itself (raft.go:242-250), the failure to transfer is attributable to the target's lacking a vote rather than to the harness or to the call. Second, it makes the cost of the vote-less attempt visible relative to the intended path: the successful transfer advanced the term by one and placed the named server in charge, while the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the campaign at term 3 and the re-election at term 4 seen in that run's log) and left the same server as a follower, so the request consumed an extra election and returned no benefit. It also corrects my earlier emphasis: transfer_err was empty in both cases, so the empty error is not what marks the failure - in the control it accompanies success. The discriminating evidence is the pair of outcomes (target_ever_leader true with one term step, versus false with two term steps) plus the two source arguments, and the caller-visible gap remains that both callers receive the same success signal while only one of them had authority moved to the named node. The current account is therefore unchanged in substance and better bounded: the defect is that the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership and reports success, and I keep the residual uncertainty about timing variation rather than smoothing it away, which is what the queued repeat of the vote-less case examines.
counterevidence: The two cases are separate executions on separate clusters, not a randomized paired trial, so run-to-run timing variation is not excluded by the pair alone; what the pair excludes is the specific alternative that the transfer mechanism does not work in this harness, and the queued repeat tests whether the vote-less non-transfer and its two-step term cost recur.
An empty transfer error occurs in both cases, so it cannot be used as the distinguishing signal; the earlier account leaned on that value and is narrowed here to the outcome and term-cost operands.

In the control the original leader ended as a follower without leading again, while in the vote-less case leadership stayed with the original server; a caller watching only the final leader could therefore see the vote-less request as harmless, and the harm is the wasted election cycle rather than a lasting loss.
limitations: Each case is a single execution with a single target chosen among followers; neither case repeats a target of the other suffrage type more than once, so the comparison rests on two runs plus the source paths.

The 3 s window bounds what is observed; the claim that a vote-less member can never win is source-based, and the term-movement comparison is an endpoint-to-endpoint difference, not a trace of every intermediate term value.

The vote-less case's target had been demoted by the caller in the same run, so the configuration change and the transfer are not separated in time in that execution; the control has no such change, which is a second difference between the two runs besides suffrage.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the vote-less case are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters of the same shape (MakeCluster(4) with default config, one elected leader, a follower chosen from Follower state as target, 3 s sampling every 20 ms). They differ in exactly one input: in the vote-less case the target is first demoted by a committed DemoteVoter, in the control it keeps its vote. They are independent executions rather than one split history, so the pair supports a same-cause comparison (transition works with a vote, does not deliver without one) and does not by itself exclude run-to-run timing variation.
